questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function
questions.problem:
The ambient temperature in a laboratory varies over time. After $t$ seconds, the temperature (in degrees Celsius) is modeled by

$$
Θ(t)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+5)+18.
$$

What is the instantaneous rate of change of the temperature as a function of $t?$

The instantaneous rate of change is
{{field-1}} degrees Celsius per second.
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the temperature is ${Θ}^{′}(t).$

We take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{Θ}^{′}(t) & =\frac{d}{dt}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+5)+18] \\  & =\frac{2}{2t+5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the ambient temperature is $\frac{2}{2t+5}$ degrees Celsius per second.

questions.problem:
The number of views $V,$ in millions, of a viral video after $t$ days is modeled by $V(t)=\frac{{10}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡10}$ for $0\le t\le 6.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of the number of views as a function of $t?$

The instantaneous rate of change is
{{field-1}} views per day.
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the number of views is equal to ${V}^{′}(t).$ 

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{10}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡10}) \\  & =\frac{{10}^{t}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡10}{\operatorname{ln}⁡10} \\  & ={10}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the number of views is ${10}^{t}.$

questions.problem: The function $P(t)=710\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{e}^{t})$ represents the volume of milk, in liters, produced on a farm $t$ days after the owner bought new cows. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the volume of produced milk as a function of $t?$
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the volume of produced milk with respect to time is ${P}^{′}(t).$

Now, the rate of change of $P(t)$ with respect to $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(710\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{e}^{t})) \\  & =710\,\frac{{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{710}{1+{e}^{-t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the volume of produced milk is  $\frac{710}{1+{e}^{-t}}$ liters per day.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function
questions.problem: The function $L(s)={s}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡s$ models the surface area of a flower's petal, in squared millimeters, as the flower's stem grows to a length of $s$ centimeters, where $s>1.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of the surface area as a function of $s?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{L}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}({s}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡s) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}({s}^{2})\operatorname{ln}⁡s+{s}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\operatorname{ln}⁡s) \\  & =(2s)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡s+{s}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{s}) \\  & =2s\operatorname{ln}⁡s+s \\  & =s(2\operatorname{ln}⁡s+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the surface area is $s(2\operatorname{ln}⁡s+1)$ squared millimeters per centimeter.

questions.problem:
The function $C(t)=6{e}^{-2t}$ gives the concentration, in milligrams per liter, of a medication in the bloodstream $t$ hours after administration. Find the instantaneous rate of change of the concentration as a function of $t.$

The instantaneous rate of change of the concentration is
{{field-1}}
milligrams per liter per hour.
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the concentration is equal to ${C}^{′}(t).$

Now, the rate of change of $C(t)$ with respect to $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{e}^{-2t}) \\  & =6(-2){e}^{-2t} \\  & =-12{e}^{-2t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the concentration is $-12{e}^{-2t}$ milligrams per liter per hour.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
questions.problem: The weight $w,$ in pounds, of a baby gorilla $t$ years after birth can be modeled by the function $w(t)=4{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+15.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of his weight when $t=1$ year?
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of weight when $t=1$ year is equal to ${w}^{′}(1).$

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{3}-{t}^{2}+15) \\  & =12{t}^{2}-2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}^{′}(1) & =12(1)^{2}-2(1) \\  & =12-2 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the weight when $t=1$ year is $10$ pounds per year.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
questions.problem: The function $x(t)={t}^{2}+t$ models the distance traveled by a car $t$ seconds after it sets off on a journey. Find the instantaneous rate at which the distance traveled by the car is changing with respect to time when $t=1$ second.
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate at which the distance traveled by the car is changing when $t=1$ second is equal to ${x}^{′}(1).$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $x(t)$ with respect to $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)=2t+1,\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $t=1$ gives

$$
{x}^{′}(1)=2(1)+1=3.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the distance traveled by the car is changing when $t=1$ second is $3$ meters per second.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
questions.problem: The function $P(v)=\frac{2v+50}{v+1}$ models the price at which gas is sold, in dollars, depending on the volume $v$ sold the previous day, in gallons. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the price of gas when $v=5$ gallons?
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the price when $v=5$ gallons is equal to ${P}^{′}(5).$

Now, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(v) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}v}(\frac{2v+50}{v+1}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}v}(2v+50)\cdot (v+1)-(2v+50)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}v}(v+1)}{(v+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2)\cdot (v+1)-(2v+50)\cdot (1)}{(v+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2v+2-2v-50}{(v+1)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{48}{(v+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $v=5$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(5) & =-\frac{48}{((5)+1)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{48}{36} \\  & =-\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the price when $v=5$ gallons is $-\frac{4}{3}$ dollars per gallon.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
questions.problem: The volume $V$ (in cubic centimeters) of water in a pail $s$ seconds after it starts filling can be modeled by the function $V(s)=7\sqrt{s}+2.$ Find the instantaneous rate at which the volume of water is changing with respect to time at the moment when the volume of water in the pail is equal to $30$ cubic centimeters.
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that the volume of water in the pail is $30$ cubic centimeters, the time can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}30 & =7\sqrt{s}+2 \\ 7\sqrt{s} & =28 \\ \sqrt{s} & =4 \\ s & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

The instantaneous rate at which the volume of water in the pail is changing when $s=16$ seconds is equal to ${V}^{′}(16).$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $V(s)$ with respect to $s$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(7\sqrt{s}+2) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(7{s}^{1/2}+2) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}{s}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{7}{2\sqrt{s}},\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $s=16$ gives

$$
{V}^{′}(16)=\frac{7}{2\sqrt{16}}=\frac{7}{8}.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the volume of water in the pail is changing when $s=16$ seconds is $\frac{7}{8}$ cubic centimeters per second.

questions.problem: A particle moves in a straight line so that after $t$ seconds it is $p(t)={t}^{3}-11t+9$ feet from its initial position. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the particle's position when $t=3$ seconds?
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the particle's position when $t=3$ seconds is equal to ${p}^{′}(3).$

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-11t+9) \\  & =3{t}^{2}-11.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, substituting $t=3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{′}(3) & =3(3)^{2}-11 \\  & =27-11 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the particle's position when $t=3$ seconds is $16$ feet per second.

questions.knowledge_point: Further Determining Rates of Change in Geometrical Settings
questions.problem:
The bases of a trapezoid are increasing and the larger base is always three times the smaller base. The height of the trapezoid is $3\,cm.$ Find the rate of change of the area of the trapezoid with respect to its smaller base $b.$

The rate of change of the area of the trapezoid with respect to its smaller base is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The area of a trapezoid is given by 

$$
A=\frac{(B+b)h}{2},
$$

 where $b$ is the smaller base, $B$ is the larger base and $h$ is the height of the trapezoid.

We are given that $B=3b$ and $h=3,$ so we can express the area $A$ as a function of the base $b$ by substituting $B=3b$ and $h=3$ in the formula above. We get

$$
A=\frac{(b+3b)(3)}{2}=6b.
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $A(b)$ with respect to $b$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(b) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}b}(6b) \\  & =6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}b}(b) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The area of the rectangle is increasing. The base of the rectangle is $b,$ and its height is $10$ times its base. Find the rate of change of the area of a rectangle with respect to its base.
questions.worked_solution:
The area of a rectangle is given by  

$$
A=bh,
$$

 where $b$ is the base and $h$ is the height of the rectangle.

We are given that $h=10b,$ so we can express the area $A$ as a function of the base $b$ by substituting $h=10b$ in the formula above. We get

$$
A=b(10b)=10{b}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $A(b)$  with respect to $b$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(b) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}b}(10{b}^{2}) \\  & =10\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}b}({b}^{2}) \\  & =10(2b) \\  & =20b.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13948186/assets/2b5d589462bf2477be3d305ea88f3d5462b7d6ea4e001a9a71790d53e1683665.png)

The area of a square is increasing. Find the instantaneous rate at which the area of a square is increasing with respect to the length of its side at the moment when the length of the sides is equal to $l=6\,\text{cm}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We know that the area of the square with respect to $l$ is given by  

$$
A=A(l)={l}^{2}.
$$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $A(l)$  with respect to $l$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(l) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}l}({l}^{2})=2l,\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $l=6$ gives

$$
{A}^{′}(6)=2(6)=12.
$$

 

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the area of the square is increasing when the length of the side is $l=6\,\text{cm}$ is $12\,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{cm}.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13948186/assets/c63dfe563c07b143bdc7cc28ab4d1142bea8c455be31ce924fa310c5e4903305.png)

The area $A$ of the circular disk above is changing as the circle expands. The circumference and radius of the circle are $C$ and $r,$ respectively. 
Find the rate of change of the area of the circle with respect to its circumference.

The rate of change of the area of the circle with respect to its circumference $C$ is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The area of a circle is given by

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2},
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the circle.

We know that $C=2\pi r,$ so we can express the area $A$ as a function of the circumference $C$ by substituting $r=\frac{C}{2\pi }$ into the formula above. We get

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $A(C)$ with respect to $C$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(C) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\  & =\frac{1}{4\pi }\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}({C}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4\pi }(2C) \\  & =\frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

The volume $V$ of the sphere above is increasing. The radius of the sphere is $r.$ Find the rate of change of the volume of a sphere with respect to its radius.
questions.worked_solution:
The volume of the sphere is given by 

$$
V=V(r)=\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3},
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the sphere.

Therefore, the rate of change of $V(r)$ with respect to $r$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\pi {r}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot 3\pi {r}^{2} \\  & =4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function
canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves in a straight line. After $t$ seconds the particle is $\, f(t)=2t^3 - 5t + 9\,$ feet away from its initial position. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the particle's position as a function of $t?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the particle's position is equal to $f'(t).$ 

We take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-5t+9) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, after $t$ seconds, the instantaneous rate of change of the particle's position is $6t^2 - 5$ feet per second.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
canonical_examples.problem: Lizzie buys $b$ pounds of bananas at a price $p,$ in dollars, that can be modeled by the function $p(b)=5e^{-0.2b}.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of the price when $b=5$ pounds?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the price when $b=5$ pounds is equal to $p'(5).$

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{′}(b) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}b}(5{e}^{-0.2b}) \\  & =5{e}^{-0.2b}\cdot (-0.2) \\  & =-{e}^{-0.2b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $b=5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{′}(5) & =-{e}^{-0.2(5)} \\  & =-{e}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the price when $b=5$ pounds is $-\dfrac{1}{e}$ dollars per pound.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Further Determining Rates of Change in Geometrical Settings
canonical_examples.problem:
A spherical balloon is being inflated so that its volume is increasing. Find the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the balloon is changing with respect to the radius at the moment when the diameter of the balloon is equal to $12\, \text{cm}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13948186/assets/e03fb046f74771676d7b1e83a1cf09176adcffaf8112e9de263404b8be74b026.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since we are given that the diameter of the balloon is $12\, \text{cm},$ its radius is $r =6\, \text{cm}.$ Now, we know that the volume of a sphere with radius $r$  is given by 

$$
V= V(r) = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3.
$$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $V(r)$  with respect to $r$ is 

$$
\eqalign{

V'(r) &= \dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d r}\left(  \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right)\[5pt]
 &  =  \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (3r^2)\[5pt]
 &= 4\pi r^2, 
}
$$

and evaluating at $r=6$ gives

$$
V'(6)=  4\pi (6)^2= 144\pi.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the balloon is changing when its diameter is $12\, \text{cm}\,$ is $\, 144\pi \, \text{cm}^3/\text{cm}.$

**Note:** We read $\text{cm}^3/\text{cm}$ as "centimeters cubed per centimeter".
